title: Physics-constrained graph closures and working-point conditioning for a fast surrogate of linac beam dynamics
summary: When a graph neural network estimates a physical quantity, its frame, edge direction, aggregation and feature normalization decide which laws it can break. Wrong choices leave systematic errors the loss never registers. We build a linac beam-dynamics surrogate on this observation. Space charge, short-range wakefields and coherent synchrotron radiation enter as bounded closures on analytic kernels, on graphs whose frame and direction follow the interaction and whose symmetry makes the net space-charge self-force vanish for any weights. Verified without training, with randomized weights, the invariants break by five to eight orders of magnitude once the responsible feature is inverted. Per-working-point models constrained by the rms envelope equation are distilled into one model conditioned on 15 machine settings. On the 18.4~m L0+L1 section of the Shanghai soft x-ray free-electron laser linac, this model predicts the transverse beam envelope at 50 unseen settings to about $7\%$, with the centroid trajectory and emittance, in 0.38~s on a single Quadro RTX 6000 GPU. Training is instead dominated by a normalization choice, a data-derived output range for the beam size: at all 16 working points it lowers the starting error 2.2- to 8.5-fold and fixes the convergence speed. The remaining accuracy differences between hybrid and data-driven architectures vary with the working point and with the density of observation. The held-out error scales roughly as $N^{-0.6}$ with the corpus size $N$. Whether the physics pays off where collective effects are strong, as in a magnetic bunch compressor, is in the next phase of our study.

title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
summary: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $κ$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.

title: Symmetry and Quantum Interference in the Attosecond Domain
summary: In this review, we examine the interplay of symmetry and quantum interference in the attosecond domain primarily through one- and two-electron photoelectron momentum distributions. Using our own work, we discuss how tailored laser fields provide control over dynamical symmetries, and how quantum-orbit methods make it possible to connect the resulting momentum-space structures to specific ionisation, propagation, and rescattering pathways. Particular emphasis is placed on ultrafast photoelectron holography and nonsequential double ionisation through recollision excitation with subsequent ionisation, where several distinct forms of quantum interference can be identified and manipulated. We also discuss how target properties, including the binding potential, orbital symmetry and parity, modify this mapping. Finally, we consider emerging opportunities offered by non-classical states of light, for which photon statistics and quantum fluctuations provide additional degrees of freedom for controlling symmetry and strong-field electron dynamics.

title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
comment: 7 pages + 1 page Supplementary Material, submitted to Europhysics Letters: Focus Issue on Complex Flows and Complex Fluids
summary: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. We discuss the root of the problem, which is intrinsic to the curved geometry rather than being a result of metric terms, coordinate system, or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.

title: Enhancing analytical photon transport in turbid media through physics-guided neural network corrections
summary: Analytical methods provide rapid and computationally efficient predictions of light transport in turbid media, making them attractive for real-time and inverse applications. However, their accuracy is limited by the approximations and assumptions used to obtain tractable solutions. On the other hand, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is widely regarded as the "gold standard" for modeling light transport in turbid media, but its high computational cost limits its use in applications requiring repeated forward evaluations. Here, we introduce a physics-guided residual learning framework that combines the computational efficiency of analytical modeling with the accuracy of MC simulation. As a representative case study, we consider the diffusion approximation (DA), which can exhibit systematic errors under relatively strong absorption, weak scattering, and imperfect boundary treatment. Given the absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, and anisotropy factor, the corresponding DA prediction is incorporated as a physical prior, while the network learns only the residual between the analytical prediction and the MC reference. Across the evaluated optical-property range, the proposed framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of approximately 62 and 14, respectively, relative to the diffusion approximation. With only 1\% of the available training data, it achieves approximately 87\% and 93\% lower corresponding errors than a direct neural-network surrogate. These results demonstrate that learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency.

title: Generation of non-Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions during thermalization of interacting baths
summary: We report on numerical experiments of thermalization between two reservoirs in which interspecies interactions are mediated via a Hamiltonian with a Gaussian dependence upon the distance between the particles. By using relatively high statistics, we are able to study deviations from the initially imprinted Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions as a function of the range and strength of the interaction, as well as the parameters of the two baths such as masses, trapping frequencies, that strongly affect the spatial overlap of the two species. At large interaction strengths and for any range, deviations are attributable to the sudden conversion of latent interaction energy into kinetic energy of the particles. In addition, long range interactions generate deviations even for interaction strengths in the weak regime, and non-uniform confinement introduces a further source of deviation from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution. This latter results in transient two temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions suggestive of an inverse cascading route from inter-particle dynamics to thermalization. In the weakly-interacting regime, a simple expression for the equilibrium temperature is also obtained and discussed. These findings may be of relevance in the dynamics of exothermic chemical reactions, in the physics of ultracold atomic mixtures, and in self-sustained burning plasmas.

title: Parallel Omnidirectional Atom Rearrangement with Dynamic Holograms
summary: The ability to assemble and reconfigure individual atoms is central to performing quantum science using optical tweezer arrays. Here, we demonstrate parallel omnidirectional atom transport and rearrangement using dynamic holograms generated by a single kilohertz-rate spatial light modulator. By carefully characterizing survival and heating, we show that atoms remain confined even when successive holograms are commanded before the liquid crystal has settled, enabling significantly faster transport. To generate holograms in real time, we develop and implement a warm-start, weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm that achieves performance comparable to neural-network methods without requiring any training. Combining these techniques, we assemble ytterbium atoms into a 2078-site kagome lattice with 99.0% mean filling. In addition, we demonstrate parallel transport between array layers, combining axial and transverse motion to reconfigure atoms in three dimensions. Our approach is readily adaptable to existing tweezer platforms and provides a method for large-scale SLM-based atom assembly as well as programmable three-dimensional control.

title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis for Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
summary: At industrial scale the cost of resolvent analysis is set by the linear solves and the assembly and storage of the Jacobian. We present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow: automatic differentiation supplies the action of the shifted Jacobian and its Hermitian transpose, preconditioned Krylov solves recycle subspaces across a Lanczos bidiagonalization, and every gain is certified by a backward error. It is applied to the NASA Common Research Model wing at Mach 0.85 and 4.2 degrees on three grid levels of 0.45, 3.6 and 28.8 million cells, the finest with 1.73x10^8 complex unknowns, 2.3 times the largest reported resolvent computation. On the coarsest level an unstable buffet mode makes the gain peak a resonance; on the finer two the operator is stable and the peak, 1.33x10^4 at omega = 6.4 and 3.0x10^3 near omega = 7.7, is a pseudo-resonance of damped modes whose buffet cells travel outboard at about 0.3 times the free-stream speed. Refinement turns an oscillator into an amplifier of the same mechanism, as forced simulations confirm. A certified frequency costs 3.6 minutes on 128 cores at 2.7 million unknowns, with 14 to 34 kB per unknown, nearly four orders of magnitude below a sparse factorization.

title: Gerchberg-Saxton Optimized Silicon Metasurface for Sinusoidal Structured-Light Three-Dimensional Imaging
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) optical imaging based on structured illumination has attracted considerable attention in applications including machine vision, robotics, and computational sensing. However, conventional structured-light systems generally rely on bulky projection components, such as digital micromirror devices and diffractive optical elements, which limit system miniaturization and integration. Here, we demonstrate a compact structured-light 3D imaging platform enabled by a silicon dielectric metasurface operating at a near-infrared wavelength of 940 nm. The desired sinusoidal fringe illumination is encoded into the metasurface through a Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) phase optimization algorithm, which converts the target far-field distribution into a nanoscale phase profile and subsequently into silicon nanopillar geometries. The fabricated metasurface generates high-quality sinusoidal structured illumination, which is integrated with a four-step phase-shifting reconstruction method to recover 3D object profiles. The proposed approach provides a compact and scalable solution for miniaturized structured-light projection and optical 3D sensing.

title: Exact Nonsymmetric Vacuum Magnetic Fields with Nested Toroidal Surfaces
summary: We give a constructive method for exact vacuum magnetic fields whose lines fill nested toroidal surfaces in ordinary space, without continuous spatial symmetry. Complex potential theory on an algebraic curve, combined with doubly periodic traveling waves from soliton theory, gives closed forms for the field, its potential and a surface label. Free parameters set the rotational transform and the magnetic shear, including exactly constant irrational transform. The same fields are exact potential flows with toroidal stream surfaces, and give stringent tests for standard stellarator codes.

title: Time-resolved Rydberg dynamics in molecules
summary: We develop a general theoretical framework for the ultrafast dynamics of coherently populated autoionizing Rydberg states in molecules, whose coherent decay results in asymmetric Fano line shapes produced by interference between resonant autoionization and direct ionization. The asymmetric line shapes form in the photoelectron continuum during the autoionization lifetime of the decreasing Rydberg population. By parameterizing autoionization resonances and solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, we model the buildup of the Fano profile together with the decline of the coherently excited Rydberg-state population. We compare our calculated photoelectron yields with the XUV-pump--IR-probe photoemission experiment of Biswas et al., Phys. Rev. A 110, 043106 (2024), in which neutral ground-state CO$_2$ molecules are excited by an XUV pulse to the Henning sharp and diffuse Rydberg series and subsequently ionized by the delayed IR pulse. Based on our numerically modeled photoelectron yields, we analyze two complementary processes: (i) photoemission into the $X^2Π_g$ continuum of residual CO$_2^+$ ions, which exposes interferences between direct photoionization and excited-state autoionization, and (ii) IR-induced photoemission into the CO$_2^+$[$B^2Σ_u^+$] continuum, which reveals quantum beats between Rydberg states. Our close-coupling model provides a versatile, extendable framework for tracking molecular Rydberg-state relaxation and, more generally, light-driven coherent dynamics in complex quantum systems.

title: FoundPDE: A generative foundation model for data-driven symbolic discovery of partial differential equations
summary: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observed data is a central inverse problem in computational science and engineering: the goal is not only to predict trajectories, but to identify interpretable symbolic laws that can be analyzed and reused. Existing PDE discovery methods often depend on hand-designed libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, or per-equation symbolic search, making them fragile under sparse observations, noisy data, broad equation families, and unseen symbolic compositions. Here, we introduce FoundPDE, a pretrained data-to-symbol foundation model for PDE discovery. FoundPDE maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectories to symbolic equations with a transformer, uses Fourier and first-order spatial-derivative augmentation to expose complementary trajectory information, refines numerical coefficients, and supports downstream extension with improved generalization through few-shot fine-tuning and hierarchical discovery. On a clean in-domain benchmark spanning 20 PDE families, our model reaches 97.50% type recognition. Under coefficient shifts beyond the training support, type recognition remains 90.53%; under multiplicative Gaussian noise on the model input, it is 94.43% at a 2% noise level but falls to 52.09% at 10%. For unseen composite equations, few-shot fine-tuning reaches over 90% exact recovery on four held-out families, and we further develop a hierarchical discovery algorithm that recovers two-term composites without fine-tuning FoundPDE. By amortizing symbolic discovery across equation families, FoundPDE shifts PDE discovery from per-dataset search toward a reusable pretrained model that extends to new physics with limited additional data, a step toward foundation models that uncover interpretable governing laws directly from scientific data.

title: Shaping the spectra of second harmonic laser by spatial focusing
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in Physical Review A
summary: Accurately controlling the spectral width of second harmonic generation (SHG) is critical in applications such as nonlinear microscopy, ultrafast spectroscopy, and quantum optics, where tailored spectral properties are required. Although it is known that the focal length of the lens used to focus the pump beam influences the SHG spectrum, a simple and precise theoretical understanding of this effect has been lacking. Here, we develop a theoretical model to describe how pump focusing conditions affect SHG spectral broadening, and experimentally validate the model using BBO crystals with lenses of 50 mm and 200 mm focal lengths. Our results establish a practical method for engineering the SHG spectral width through pump focusing, providing valuable guidance for designing nonlinear optical systems with specific spectral requirements.

title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
summary: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

title: Allight: A Perfect Photon Collector
summary: Collecting photons from quantum emitters remains a key limitation in light-matter interaction because conventional lenses collect light only from one direction. Here, we introduce a perfect light collector by inverse-designing a surrounding dielectric structure that encloses the emitter to increase photon-collection efficiency toward unity. Decomposing the device into several refractive interfaces enables emission collection from the full 4$π$ solid angle with adiabatic reshaping into a collimated beam. We experimentally demonstrate, in two dimensions, the ray bending that collimates omnidirectional emission. Our collector transforms current paradigms for highly efficient photon collection from narrowband, cavity-based techniques into experimentally robust, broadband, non-resonant dielectric devices.

title: Triadic energy routes in a short laminar separation bubble
comment: 28 pages, 18 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: The kinetic energy budget of a laminar separation bubble on a compressor blade is formed mode by mode in frequency and spanwise wavenumber from a direct numerical simulation at a Reynolds number of $2.5\times10^{5}$ based on the axial chord. The nonlinear transfer between modes is evaluated as a triadic tensor that gives the energy exchanged in every triad, the roles of its three modes, and the location of the exchange. Nine dominant tonal modes are identified: the flapping of the bubble, the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode with its sidebands, a pair of modes near reattachment, and their sum, difference, and harmonic. They hold 8% of the fluctuation energy, and their triads are responsible for 19% of the energy exchanged. Every tonal mode is fed by the mean shear and exports 69 to 82% of the energy it takes from the mean flow. The Kelvin-Helmholtz mode sends 45% of the energy it sheds to lower frequencies. The largest of these transfers is a triad in which it acts as a catalyst. The exchange in each triad is split into nine channels by velocity components. In every triad of spanwise-uniform modes, one channel dominates: the wall-tangential velocity of the donor advected by the wall-normal velocity of the catalyst. For a pair of oblique modes, the same advection by the two-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz mode exchanges their spanwise velocity, which the mean flow cannot produce. The rollers thus become three-dimensional through the advecting velocity of the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode, which supplies no energy to the exchange.

title: Machine-learned spectral PDE solvers for fluids and plasmas
summary: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.

title: Machine-learned spectral PDE solvers for fluids and plasmas
summary: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.

title: Controlling Optical Quantum Interference with Plasmonic Metasurfaces
summary: The ability to efficiently control optical quantum interference by the same device is a challenging task that promises to enable key operations in quantum information processing. Here, we tackle this problem by presenting a composite quantum plasmonic metasurface operating as an ultrathin non-unitary beamsplitter capable of achieving both single photon bosonic bunching and fermionic anti-bunching interference just by varying the incident photons frequency or changing the design dimensions. The presented metasurface combines a plasmonic grating corrugated by periodic nanoslits that can achieve extraordinary optical transmission with additional nanostripes on top forming nanocavities characterized by localized gap plasmon resonances. The photon-photon interactions are analyzed based on calculating the quantum coalescence metric which accurately portrays the obtained bunching or anti-bunching quantum interference. The presented quantum interference operation is applicable to both fundamental non-classical light interactions and in the design of more applied quantum optical logic gates used in quantum computing and communications.

title: A Neural Implicit Flow Super-Resolution Approach for Reacting Flows
summary: We present a novel framework for reconstructing fine-resolution scalar fields from coarse-resolution data in 2D unsteady flames using an extension of neural implicit flow (NIF). The framework leverages the novel architecture of NIF to develop an efficient representation of scalar fields in spatio-temporal reacting flows. Different strategies are adopted within the proposed framework to establish super-resolution for multiscalar fields in combustion. They include 1) a reconfiguration of the input and output fields, 2) the use of a latent composition space based on nonlinear principal component analysis (NLPCA) to reconstruct the fine-resolution fields, and the conversion from nonlinear principal components (NLPCs) to species and temperature contours, and 3) the adoption of multiple ParameterNets in the NIF architecture, each accommodating one of the NLPCs. The framework was validated on a 2D unsteady Bunsen-stabilized lean premixed methane-air flame with forcing at the inlet. The results, using a coarsening ratio of 8 in a given direction, show that the adoption of multiple ParameterNets yields more accurate super-resolution than a single ParameterNet without any additional cost in the hyperparameters.

title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
comment: Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. E as a Letter
summary: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

title: Proper generalized decomposition with synthetic preconditioning for multiscale parametric phonon transport
summary: Deterministic solution of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation is costly for two reasons: the distribution depends on high-dimensional phase space, and source iteration converges slowly when scattering is frequent. We address both for the steady linearized gray Callaway model in two dimensions by combining proper generalized decomposition (PGD) with the general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS). The distribution is a sum of products of a space--azimuth factor and a polar factor. This splitting is intrinsically low-rank: along each characteristic the polar angle only stretches the in-plane optical depth, so the rank is bounded, uniformly in the Knudsen numbers, by the numerical rank of the kernel $\exp(-τ/\sinφ)$. PGD--GSIS updates the factors against a macroscopic source frozen within each alternating step and refreshed by the GSIS moment equations. A Fourier analysis shows that pure PGD, although implicit in the polar factor, moves macroscopic information only through lagged spatial sweeps and stalls like source iteration, whereas the synthetic refresh sees only third-order moments of the representation error. On an isothermal cavity, cross-plane conduction and phonon Poiseuille flow, PGD--GSIS reproduces full-order solutions at ranks 3--14, with heat-flux errors below $6\times10^{-3}$ from the diffusive to the ballistic regime and memory independent of the polar resolution. Treating the inverse Knudsen numbers as coordinates of the polar factor yields one spatial basis over four decades of both; a joint update of all polar factors, which costs only small nodal linear systems, is required for accuracy at large Knudsen numbers.

title: The optical force on a dielectric slab
summary: Radiation-pressure forces on transmissive optics, including dynamical backaction, are usually computed from the momentum flux of the external fields. For a dielectric of finite thickness, this omits the time dependence of the electromagnetic momentum stored inside. We compute the force on a lossless dielectric slab of arbitrary thickness $L_s$ submerged in a dielectric fluid, proceeding from both Lorentz force on its bound charges and from the external momentum fluxes for arbitrary carrier and sideband fields. We treat the surrounding medium through a prescribed linear dielectric response and do not model the accompanying mechanical response of the fluid, including pressure and electrostriction. These two methods both recover the expected force in the limit of a thin reflector, but differ in the more general case by the rate of change of the field momentum stored in the slab. This storage term vanishes for static fields and at low frequencies reduces to $(L_s/c^2)\,dP/dt$, where $P$ is the net power through the slab. In a cavity, where $P$ depends on the slab position, the storage term produces a velocity-dependent force. The Abraham and Minkowski momentum formulations applied to the storage term are reconciled to give an unambiguous force on the dielectric in the case of an exterior vacuum environment, where there is no fluid response to model.

title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations
summary: We present a perturbation-based theoretical framework, together with its immersed boundary/volume penalization implementation, for long-time simulations of fully resolved rigid-particle dynamics in acoustically actuated flows. A perturbation formulation separates the fast acoustic time scale from the slow mean dynamics, avoiding long-time direct integration of the fully compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The immersed rigid body is represented through a Brinkman penalization term in equations posed over a unified fluid-solid domain. The coupled fluid-particle system is decomposed into a time-harmonic first-order problem governing the acoustic response and a time-averaged second-order problem. A central challenge in this decomposition is the treatment of the moving fluid-solid interface. We derive order-consistent expressions for the structural velocities, comprising rigid-body and Stokes-drift contributions, and formulate the corresponding first- and second-order rigid-body equations of motion. For a circular particle in two dimensions, the simulations reveal substantial differences in the magnitude and structure of acoustic streaming around fixed and freely moving particles, highlighting the importance of two-way fluid-structure coupling. The results also show that particle-density effects are more complex than suggested by simplified descriptions based solely on the acoustic contrast factor. The framework captures the mean particle dynamics using time steps associated with the slow particle-motion scale rather than the much smaller acoustic time scale. Finally, simulations of an elliptical particle demonstrate the ability of the method to capture coupled translational and rotational motion. The proposed approach therefore provides an efficient route to fully resolved, long-time simulations of acoustically driven rigid-particle motion while retaining two-way fluid-structure coupling.

title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
summary: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.

title: Nanophotonic Extreme Ultraviolet Polarimeter
summary: Nanophotonic engineering has revolutionized how we manipulate the polarization of visible light. Here, we extend such control to extreme ultraviolet radiation, the spectral region of attosecond science and semiconductor lithography, where transmissive optical elements are lacking. We implement channel waveguides that restrict incident 41-nm-wavelength light to a few modes with defined spatial profiles and propagation constants. By designing the propagation-length-dependent interference of two eigenmodes, we achieve polarization-dependent forward scattering, which we exploit to create a transmissive nanophotonic analyzer that resolves the polarization axis and spectrum of extreme ultraviolet light from a single measurement. With a 0.9°-sensitivity for polarization rotations in a 1-second measurement and single-shot capability, the device opens new experimental opportunities in ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy and at accelerator-based light sources.

title: NeRF-Inspired Neural Fields for 3D Super-resolution of Reacting-Flows
summary: The multiscale nature of turbulent reacting flows and the importance of fine-scale structures pose challenges for super-resolution. We investigate a 3D super-resolution framework inspired by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), called Neural Field Super-Resolution (NFSR), to reconstruct fine-resolution fields from coarsened reacting-flow fields. The proposed formulation adapts the continuous coordinate-conditioned representation of NeRF to physical flow-field reconstruction by conditioning spatial coordinates with local coarse-grid thermochemical information, while eliminating radiance prediction and volume rendering. Principal component analysis is used to provide a compact and low-dimensional representation of the thermochemical state, and a hierarchical extension, H-NFSR, progressively reconstructs the solution through intermediate resolution levels. The framework is evaluated using three-dimensional direct numerical simulation data for a turbulent premixed hydrogen-air flame, with an overall spatial coarsening factor of eight in each coordinate direction. The results demonstrate consistently better prediction measures and a higher ability to reconstruct fine-scale information than tricubic interpolation on the unseen test realization. The hierarchical formulation reduces visible coarse-cell imprinting. In contrast, biased sampling mainly benefits the most localized structures. Three-dimensional isosurface comparisons further show that H-NFSR recovers much of the small and intermediate features of the flow, including surface wrinkling and local flame curvature effects. These results highlight the potential of coordinate-conditioned neural fields as a flexible framework for three-dimensional coarse-to-fine reconstruction of reacting-flow simulations.

title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
summary: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $κ$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.

title: From random patterns to nanophotonic structures: Electromagnetic field prediction without retraining
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 1 table; Supporting Information: 49 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables
summary: Electromagnetic surrogate solvers can accelerate nanophotonic design, but their broader use requires accurate predictions for unseen geometries and material arrangements. Training on random dielectric patterns enables direct prediction of complex electromagnetic fields in diverse two-dimensional nanophotonic structures without retraining. The network takes spatial permittivity distributions as inputs, with training samples drawn from a dataset comprising 700,140 combinations of 5,001 random freeform dielectric patterns and 140 relative permittivities from 2.1 to 16.0. The trained model predicts fields for aperiodic bar arrays, manually defined patterns, inverse-designed metalenses, inverse-designed binary structures, and two-material freeform patterns excluded from training. Across 35,441 geometry-permittivity samples, a dilated residual network achieves average relative field errors of 1.4%-7.6%. For 6,950 inverse-designed metalens samples, the three most accurate architectures predict transmitted power with median relative errors of 0.7%-0.9%. Accuracy depends on refractive index and structural scale, with greater errors for patterns coarser than those used for training. These results demonstrate transfer to independently constructed geometries and to new spatial arrangements of dielectric values not represented in the training. Random-pattern training therefore supports reuse of electromagnetic surrogates across multiple structural families, providing a basis for sharing training costs among material screening, iterative optical design, and fabrication-tolerance analysis.

title: Formation of a Vorticity Singularity in an Axisymmetric Poloidal Flow
summary: In this work, building on previous studies of plane-parallel flows, we investigate the rapid growth of the frozen-in vorticity field in an axisymmetric poloidal flow. We present the results of numerical simulations performed using supercomputing resources. We show that exponentially growing velocity gradients can develop on the axis of symmetry, while vorticity gradients grow superexponentially. These results are qualitatively similar to those previously obtained for vorticity in a simpler two-dimensional flow.

title: Generation of non-Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions during thermalization of interacting baths
summary: We report on numerical experiments of thermalization between two reservoirs in which interspecies interactions are mediated via a Hamiltonian with a Gaussian dependence upon the distance between the particles. By using relatively high statistics, we are able to study deviations from the initially imprinted Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions as a function of the range and strength of the interaction, as well as the parameters of the two baths such as masses, trapping frequencies, that strongly affect the spatial overlap of the two species. At large interaction strengths and for any range, deviations are attributable to the sudden conversion of latent interaction energy into kinetic energy of the particles. In addition, long range interactions generate deviations even for interaction strengths in the weak regime, and non-uniform confinement introduces a further source of deviation from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution. This latter results in transient two temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions suggestive of an inverse cascading route from inter-particle dynamics to thermalization. In the weakly-interacting regime, a simple expression for the equilibrium temperature is also obtained and discussed. These findings may be of relevance in the dynamics of exothermic chemical reactions, in the physics of ultracold atomic mixtures, and in self-sustained burning plasmas.

title: Controlling exceptional points of layered non-Hermitian structures with magnetic field
summary: Exceptional points are the characteristic features of non-Hermitian systems providing numerous applications in optics, acoustics, electronics, etc. We show that exceptional points can be controlled with the external magnetic field by considering the archetypal three-layered $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric photonic structure including a magneto-optic material between the loss and gain layers. Application of the magnetic field makes the system anisotropic with the polarization-sensitive reflection and transmission properties. As a result, the magnetic field can stimulate $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking and mode exchange at realistic values of system parameters. Moreover, we suggest that the proposed scheme can be also used for magnetic-perturbation sensing with an easily adaptable level of desired field strength. Our results contain a valuable evidence for the usefulness of anisotropic (including magnetic) materials for tunable non-Hermitian photonics.

title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow
summary: The evolution of finite-amplitude disturbances is critical in the prediction of laminar-to-turbulent transition. To analyze the transient growth of disturbances, Pralits et al. (J. Fluid Mechanics, 2015) proposed a weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation (WNLOP) analysis that accounts for the effect of mean-flow distortion on the fundamental wave. The present study formulates a WNLOP analysis via Picard--Chebyshev iteration for compressible parallel flows to predict streak breakdown. The formulation incorporates the non-modal amplification of disturbances and their nonlinear interactions for polychromatic waves, considering all the possible nonlinear interactions starting from a finite set of initial wavenumber components. The nonlinear interaction is tracked as a monotonically increasing set of wavenumber components; specifically, the first-order approximation recovers the linear disturbance equation, the third-order approximation corresponds to the amplitude equation of weakly nonlinear theory, and further iterations systematically approach DNS results in the weakly nonlinear regime. By applying the proposed formulation to a subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach number $\mathrm{M}=0.3$ and Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=3000$, the proposed formulation demonstrates high predictive accuracy in comparison with DNS calculations and succeeds in identifying the optimal perturbation restricted to a planar wave that causes streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation. The proposed method predicts the nonlinear interaction between the streak and the planar wave, which generates an oblique wave and subsequent harmonic waves characterized by an alternating streamwise vortex structure, whose amplitude determines whether further nonlinear interactions are induced to trigger the turbulent transition.

title: Enhanced orbital-angular-momentum dimensionality and spatial-spectral decoupling in thin-film SPDC
summary: Thin-film spontaneous parametric down-conversion, due to the relaxed phase-matching condition, generates photon pairs that are extremely broadband in frequency and angle and highly entangled in time/frequency and position/momentum. Here we show that it also provides a very broad orbital angular momentum (OAM) spectrum, which, in contrast to the case of bulk crystals, is decoupled from the frequency spectrum. To demonstrate it experimentally, we generate photon pairs in a $7~μ\mathrm{m}$-thick lithium niobate film and compare them with those from a $500~μ\mathrm{m}$-thick periodically poled lithium niobate crystal under identical pump conditions. The thin-film source exhibits a substantially broader OAM spectrum, with the azimuthal Schmidt number almost 9 times larger than that of the bulk source. On this highly entangled state, we perform quantum-state tomography in selected two- and four-dimensional OAM subspaces, demonstrating high-purity maximally entangled states. These results highlight thin nonlinear films as a promising platform for high-dimensional quantum-state generation with weak spatial--spectral coupling.

title: Influence of Ideal, Cubic, and Multiparameter Helmholtz Equations of State on the Static and Dynamic Performance of Porous Aerostatic Journal Bearings
summary: Porous aerostatic gas bearings are commonly modeled using the ideal-gas law, although non-ideal thermodynamic behavior may become relevant for alternative working fluids. This study quantifies the influence of the thermodynamic closure on the stationary and dynamic response of porous aerostatic journal bearings. A finite-volume formulation couples the compressible Reynolds equation with three-dimensional Darcy flow, retaining transient gas storage in both domains. Density is used as the primary thermodynamic variable, allowing the ideal-gas, van der Waals, Soave--Redlich--Kwong, Peng--Robinson, and multiparameter Helmholtz equations of state to be evaluated within an otherwise unchanged bearing model. Air, R1234yf, and R1234ze(E) are considered. For air, EOS-induced differences remain negligible over the investigated range. For the refrigerants, the ideal-gas approximation produces several-percent deviations, with supplied mass flow and dynamic force response being particularly sensitive. The cubic equations substantially reduce these deviations, with the employed Peng--Robinson formulation providing the closest agreement with the Helmholtz reference for both refrigerants at a computational cost comparable to the other cubic models. The results identify density and differential compressibility as the main thermodynamic quantities governing the propagation of EOS errors into mass transport and transient gas storage.

title: Attosecond Quantum Optical Spectroscopy of Topological Materials
summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) provides an ultrafast probe of quantum materials, yet conventional spectral observables do not generally furnish a common signature of band topology. Here we show that quantum-light-driven HHG opens an additional information channel through the photon statistics of the emitted harmonics. Using the Haldane Chern insulator and the time-reversal-invariant Kane-Mele topological insulator, we calculate helicity-resolved equal-time intensity correlations and identify a common enhancement of high-order harmonic correlations in the topological phases. For the Haldane model, a dichroic correlation constructed from opposite helicity channels reverses sign with the Chern number. These signatures originate from the distinct nonlinear response sampled by quantum fluctuations of the driving field and are absent from the corresponding mean harmonic spectra as a common classifier. Our results establish photon-correlation spectroscopy as a route to interrogate topological matter with quantum light and provide a bridge between strong-field solid-state physics and quantum optics.

title: Second-order difference-frequency effects on floating wind turbine responses: full-QTF modelling and experimental comparison
comment: 33 pages, submitted to Applied Ocean Research
summary: Accurate prediction of low-frequency responses is important for the dynamic assessment of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs), as second-order difference-frequency wave loads can contribute substantially to platform motions and mooring loads. Their relative importance, however, remains less well established when aerodynamic and hydrodynamic low-frequency excitations coexist under operating conditions. This study develops an efficient time-domain formulation for full difference-frequency quadratic transfer function (QTF) loading using bandwidth truncation and integrates it into a fully coupled model of the IEA 15 MW turbine on the VolturnUS-S semi-submersible platform. Numerical predictions are compared with 1:70-scale real-time hybrid wave-basin experiments covering both irregular wave-only and combined turbulent wind-wave conditions. Three hydrodynamic formulations are compared: linear wave excitation, Newman's approximation, and the full-QTF model. Under wave-only conditions, second-order difference-frequency loading substantially improves the prediction of surge and the associated mooring response, particularly in energetic sea states, with the full-QTF model generally providing the closest agreement with measured low-frequency spectra and peak-amplitude distributions. Under combined wind-wave conditions, low-frequency thrust fluctuations dominate near rated wind speed, reducing the relative importance of difference-frequency wave excitation, whereas its contribution becomes more apparent at higher wind speeds as thrust fluctuations diminish. Overall, the full-QTF model provides the most consistent improvement over the linear and Newman models, with maximum surge standard deviation discrepancy from measurement under the most energetic wave conditions less than 18%, with smaller discrepancies for heave, pitch, and mooring tensions.

title: Quantum Limits of Blind Superresolution Imaging
summary: Quantum estimation has shown that spatial-mode measurements can avoid Rayleigh's curse, but the fundamental precision limits are usually formulated for a known point-spread function (PSF). We show that, for two equally bright incoherent sources sharing an unknown static, shift-invariant complex-amplitude response, the local quantum information for separation is exactly the same as in the known-PSF case. In a quantum semiparametric formulation, the equality follows from the orthogonality of the separation score to the nuisance tangent space generated by all admissible PSF perturbations. We propose two receivers to access this information: momentum-resolved Hong--Ou--Mandel interference (MR-HOM), which acquires half the small-separation quantum information per signal photon without reconstructing the PSF, and a tomography-assisted symmetric logarithmic derivative receiver (TA-SLD), which asymptotically attains the full bound under explicit recovery conditions. These results provide a route toward blind superresolution without prior PSF calibration in microscopy, astronomy, and other optical imaging systems with uncertain responses.

title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
comment: Accepted for publication in Experiments in Fluids
summary: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_τ= 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $δ$ for the onset transient and $0.9δ$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5δ$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.

title: Dual Transverse Vortex-Spin-Momentum Locking in Rotating-Wave Structured Light
summary: We theoretically investigate the transverse Poynting momentum and transverse spin angular momentum in circularly polarized rotating-wave structured light, and reveal a pair of \emph{dual} transverse vortex-spin-momentum locking. The transverse Poynting momentum exhibits a $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetric locking structure, being controlled independently by either the polarization or vortex handedness, yet invariant under their simultaneous reversal. Meanwhile, the transverse spin angular momentum is independent of the polarization but endowed with a crucial vortex-dependence inheriting such vortex-dependence from the Poytning momentum via curl operation. This finding expands the understanding of transverse optical linear and angular momenta in structured light and opens a new paradigm for vortex-spin-controlled optical manipulation.

title: Wavepackets in subsonic elliptical jets: coherent-structure eduction and linear modelling
summary: We study coherent structures extracted from time-resolved particle image velocimetry (TR-PIV) measurements of isothermal elliptical jets with aspect ratio of 1:2, at Mach numbers 0.4 and 0.7. The velocity snapshots are decomposed according to the D$_2$ symmetry. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) is then used to identify coherent structures. Modelling is performed using three-dimensional parabolised stability equations (3D-PSE) based on linearisation about the time-averaged mean flows. A comparison between SPOD and 3D-PSE results shows alignment of SPOD and single-mode PSE structures of up to 70\%. A linear combination of PSE solutions, obtained from the family of initially unstable local modes, leads to SPOD-PSE alignment of up to 90\%. Limitations are observed at low frequencies and near the nozzle and are attributed to the existence of non-modal amplification mechanisms. The study shows that coherent structures in turbulent elliptical jets can be educed using the D$_2$-SPOD approach, and modelled using 3D PSE.

title: Continuously Tunable Mid-Infrared Metalens Integrating Moiré and Pancharatnam-Berry Phases
summary: A varifocal mid-infrared metalens designed for focusing applications is proposed to integrate both Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) and Moiré pattern-based mechanisms for rotational wavefront control. The metalens employs two identical nanostructured discs featuring germanium (Ge) meta-atoms on calcium fluoride (CaF2) substrates, operating as birefringent half-wave retarders with 99.95% Polarization Conversion Ratio (PCR) and 83.65% total transmission power at 2 μm wavelength. Full-wave numerical simulations demonstrate continuous focal length tunability from 45 μm to 12 μm by rotating the second disk from 30 deg. to 120 deg., corresponding to the numerical aperture values ranging from 22.99% to 68.67%. The proposed metalens maintains reconfigurable focusing regardless of the incident light polarization, while concurrently enabling polarization-controlled operation via a phase-modulation mechanism that yields inverse responses under Right Circular Polarization (RCP) and Left Circular Polarization (LCP) illuminations.

title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
comment: Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. E as a Letter
summary: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

title: Mechanically reconfigurable layered GRIN lenses for mid-infrared
summary: This paper presents a concept of mechanically adjustable planar Gradientindex (GRIN) lens that can be used to realize reconfigurable focusing at mid-infrared (mid-IR) or millimeter-wave (mm-wave) frequencies. The concept is based on a multilayer design rooted in effective medium theory, where spatial refractive index profiles are synthesized using first-kind Chebyshev polynomials. Symmetric lateral displacement of the layers enables continuous modulation of the effective refractive index distribution, allowing controlled transitions between divergent, afocal, and convergent wavefronts. Numerical simulations demonstrate accurate focal tuning at mid-IR and mm-waves. In the mid-IR regime, focal lengths of about 56 μm and 24 μm are achieved with relative errors of around 4.4% and 10%, respectively. In the mm-wave regime, the lens produces focal lengths of about 158 mm and 128 mm with improved accuracies of 2.3% and 6.0%, respectively. The reconstructed refractive index profiles exhibit high similarity to ideal convex lens distributions, confirming the validity of the proposed synthesis approach. The proposed GRIN lens concept offers a scalable and physically interpretable approach to reconfigurable focusing, with potential applications in multimodal imaging, adaptive sensing, and telecommunication systems.

title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows
summary: A graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder is leveraged to produce reduced latent graph representations of detonation-containing flows. In a two-dimensional hydrogen-air channel configuration with a uniform fuel-air mixture, it was found that latent graphs with effective resolutions of twice the induction length are capable of reconstructing both the wavefront and the post-shock region of the cellular detonation wave structure. Extrapolation studies using stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations revealed an intrinsic property of GNN-based reconstruction from reduced latent graphs -- a representational hierarchy, rooted in the local nature of message passing, that tends to prioritize features at the detonation front (i.e., the wavefront profile and triple points) over the downstream deflagrative regions. In particular, it was found that at a fixed ambient condition, the information contained in uniform two-dimensional detonations was sufficient to reconstruct the wavefront structure of both stratified and three-dimensional detonations. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of GNNs for both reduction and information overlap extraction in detonation-containing flows, opening promising pathways for accelerated simulations of these flows.

title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis for Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
summary: At industrial scale the cost of resolvent analysis is set by the linear solves and the assembly and storage of the Jacobian. We present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow: automatic differentiation supplies the action of the shifted Jacobian and its Hermitian transpose, preconditioned Krylov solves recycle subspaces across a Lanczos bidiagonalization, and every gain is certified by a backward error. It is applied to the NASA Common Research Model wing at Mach 0.85 and 4.2 degrees on three grid levels of 0.45, 3.6 and 28.8 million cells, the finest with 1.73x10^8 complex unknowns, 2.3 times the largest reported resolvent computation. On the coarsest level an unstable buffet mode makes the gain peak a resonance; on the finer two the operator is stable and the peak, 1.33x10^4 at omega = 6.4 and 3.0x10^3 near omega = 7.7, is a pseudo-resonance of damped modes whose buffet cells travel outboard at about 0.3 times the free-stream speed. Refinement turns an oscillator into an amplifier of the same mechanism, as forced simulations confirm. A certified frequency costs 3.6 minutes on 128 cores at 2.7 million unknowns, with 14 to 34 kB per unknown, nearly four orders of magnitude below a sparse factorization.

title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
summary: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
summary: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.
